title: Turlov: Chess is massively undervalued
summary:
Before Timur Turlov’s election to FIDE President his role in FIDE was growing. His company, Freedom Holding Corp. , had already become FIDE’s principal sponsor; his Kazakhstan Chess Federation had staged the 2023 World Championship match in Astana and put the World Rapid and Blitz on Wall Street.

He is aware of how his rapid rise within FIDE may look, and has decided it works in his favor. “I’m still not the most familiar person for the chess community,” he said in an interview conducted by video link in early August. “I hope we will use every opportunity to meet each other and talk to each other before this election happens. And I hope that I still will be able to surprise many delegates... Don’t just try to think in stereotypes. Sometimes it’s better to talk than not to talk.”

Lobnya to Wall Street

Turlov was born in 1987 in Lobnya, a town outside Moscow near Sheremetyevo airport. His early years were shaped by the dramatic changes that followed the collapse of the Soviet Union. He grew up in a rapidly changing Russia, at a time when the country was finding its way into a new era.

What he wanted was the world he saw in American movies. “No one had a home like that in Moscow,” he has said of the suburban house in Home Alone. Wall Street films left a different mark: wealthy people in them, he noticed, “did something with the stock market.”

He opened his first brokerage account at about fourteen with roughly $800 inherited from his grandfather, and lost most of it. At sixteen he was interning at an American firm in Moscow, attending school in the mornings and trading until midnight while New York was open — “high-frequency trading before it became algo-based,” as he describes it. He joined Uniastrum Bank’s brokerage arm in 2005 and was out of a job at twenty-one when the bank collapsed in 2008, despite his own desk remaining profitable to the last day.

He and six colleagues pooled their severance — roughly $100,000 — and started again. That company became Freedom Holding.

He moved the business to Kazakhstan in 2011, on a friend’s recommendation, and discovered a family connection: his father had been born in Shymkent. He has lived in Almaty for over a decade with his wife and six children. Freedom listed on Nasdaq in October 2019, the first financial company from Russia or Central Asia to list there, and Turlov rang the bell himself. He became a Kazakh citizen in June 2022, after the invasion of Ukraine, and ceased to hold Russian citizenship. The company sold its Russian subsidiaries the following February.

Freedom Holding reported revenue of $2.19 billion for the fiscal year ended March 2026, and Forbes ranks Turlov among Kazakhstan’s wealthiest individuals. Its consumer “super app” — banking, brokerage, insurance, travel, ticketing, groceries, film streaming — serves more than 11mn customers across more than twenty countries. That product, more than the balance sheet, shapes how he thinks about running a federation.

How He Came to Chess

Turlov plays. So do all six of his children, including a daughter who could push the pieces at three. “I play with them at dinner time or on weekends or when travelling,” he said in an earlier interview in Almaty. “They sometimes have decent results in local competitions, but they don’t take it seriously — it’s just a hobby.” He added: “For now.”

“Chess is massively undervalued”

Turlov wants to turn its global reach

into a bigger opportunity for sponsors.

He took over the Kazakhstan Chess Federation in 2023, and the results since have been hard to argue with. Kazakh players won 162 international medals in 2025, 64 of them gold. The women’s team took silver at the Budapest Olympiad. Bibisara Assaubayeva has three world blitz titles. Edgar Mamedov became the country’s youngest-ever grandmaster at fourteen and is the reigning U16 world champion. Danis Kuandykuly, the U12 world champion, drew with Magnus Carlsen at Grenke.

Underneath the elite results sits a schools program in more than 1,500 Kazakh schools reaching over 60,000 children, plus a donation of about KZT 20mn to bring chess into fifty orphanages. Turlov is also president of the International School Chess Federation, a body he proposed and the FIDE General Assembly approved.

Companies associated with him have put more than $75mn into the game, at a rate he has described as $10mn to $20mn per year. Asked in Almaty why he had gotten into chess, he put the business case second.

“First and foremost it is my passion and charity — why I came to chess,” he said. “The marketing and the relationships we develop through chess — I think that is just a side effect. Because chess opened a lot of doors in the banking world. It is a very nice, high-quality club of people.”

He is candid that the club is also the pitch. “Chess is massively undervalued. A lot of chess fans are intellectual people. It’s bankers, politicians, business leaders, different artists,” he said this summer. Businesses are “missing a great opportunity for sponsorship. With relatively small budgets, you can get global influence.”

What He Would Actually Do

His central claim is that FIDE governs the professional game competently but captures almost none of the value from the game’s migration online — and that federations will never be financially secure until they do. “Funding for federations will never be secure or sustainable unless we have a much stronger presence online,” he said.

In practice that means CRM systems so each federation can count its players; a chess ID, modeled on the KazChess ID already being completed in Kazakhstan, so a federation knows who in its country plays; voluntary accreditation of clubs, so a parent can tell a beginners’ club from a professionals’ one; calendar alignment tools; arbiter registries with allocation; performance tracking. A single platform, in other words, sitting underneath 200 federations of widely varying capacity.

Then he goes further than any other candidate has. He wants “a very strong link between online gaming platforms and national federations,” he said — “starting with biometric identification of chess players to maintain the integrity of ratings.”

For a readership that has spent five years arguing about online fair play, that is the most consequential statement in the interview. It is also the least developed. He did not specify what would be captured, by whom, under what privacy regime, or whether the major platforms have agreed to anything. No other candidate is proposing it.

The second surprise is the Olympics, which appear nowhere in the five pillars his campaign published on August 1.

“We need to become an Olympic sport, and I think we have a very good chance to become an Olympic sport,” he said. “It’s not fast, but at least I want to come as close as possible to this moment in the next four years.” The route runs through continental recognition: “We need recognition from international competitions such as the Asian Games, European Games and African Games.”

The barrier, as he sees it, is not participation. “Hundreds of millions of people play chess in the world and it’s enough for the Olympics for sure,” he said. It is that chess is close to unwatchable for people who do not play it.

“Sometimes to really understand all beauty you need to be at least a master to understand the beauty of grandmasters,” he said. “With the help of AI, we can make broadcasts more attractive to the general public” — including, he suggested, “at least some beautiful animation of different lines.” A research group has been set up to work on it.

Third, and perhaps the most immediately practical, money with a longer horizon. He wants to underwrite FIDE’s calendar so events can be scheduled two years out.

“My key is to provide some financial backstop to FIDE, to make sure that we will be able to plan a longer calendar,” he said. The problem, in his diagnosis, is not staffing: “That happens not just because of a lack of professionals. That happens because of lack of predictability.”

He also wants federations to be able to embed chess in other businesses without building the technology themselves — essentially, a software development kit, so a national federation can strike a deal with a bank or a telecom. Asked whether people might one day solve puzzles to pay for things, he did not hesitate. “Yes, why not? You can give some gigabytes for solving puzzles, some extra internet, some extra engagement.”

His warning to federations that ignore all this is blunt: “They will lose authority over this game.”

ChessBase, and the Freedom Ecosystem

In April, Freedom acquired ChessBase — the Hamburg company whose databases have been the working infrastructure of professional chess for four decades — with about €5mn of committed investment. The headquarters stay in Hamburg, the management team stays, no job cuts are planned, and the group expects to add staff. The plan is to upgrade the platform with AI and connect it to the super app. ChessBase managing director Rainer Woisin called the deal “a secure new stage of development.”

The acquisition is the clearest expression of how Turlov thinks. His argument for the super app is also his argument for FIDE.

“Each big organization is kind of similar sometimes even to a small country,” he said. “So if you want to manage your country properly, you need to take care of multiple disciplines.” Ecosystems beat standalone products because the pieces reinforce each other: shared identity, shared payment rails, shared data. Applied to chess, that means the whole pyramid — schools at the base, then clubs, then tournaments, then the professional game — with one digital spine running through it and federations taught to raise money and explain themselves to governments and sponsors.

Whether the model exports is the open question. It rests in Kazakhstan on infrastructure most FIDE members do not have: a national digital ID system Turlov rates among the world’s best, and a country where 85% of payments are already cashless. He did not address how it would work in federations without any of that.

Chess and Decision-Making

Turlov has no interest in political office. “I truly believe that now I will be much more useful for any society and for any country as a businessman,” he said. “And frankly, I will be much more free in my decisions.”

What he offers instead is a promise to deliver. “If we’re promising something, we are from business, we are not from politics. We know how important it is to deliver what was promised.”

He is also clear, at least rhetorically, about the limits of the office. “We will never change the chessboard without deep involvement of the National Federation,” he said. “Any single person with any resource will not change. The community will do this.”

On the schools programs he is unromantic about outcomes. “Chess in school programs is not just to make grandmasters. Sometimes it’s just to let people study better,” he said. “Maybe they will never become even a master... Even they will become a doctor and will play chess with their kids. It’s also okay.”

A year ago, asked what the game had taught him, he talked about tiredness and consequences: do not decide when exhausted, and consider the opponent’s reply rather than only your own move. Asked the same question this summer, the answer had moved.

“In management, especially for organizations like FIDE, your mistakes are usually in your relationships with different people,” he said. “A lot of chess players actually don’t care so much about relationships. They’re more focused on results of their game... But in federation, you need to be focused on relationships. That’s all we do.”

“Mistakes could not be just factual,” he added. “Mistakes also could be in your relationships. And also if you’re tired and sick, so don’t clash with your people, with your friends, with your colleagues, with your community.”

The above interview was conducted by Leon Aris , a foreign correspondent

additionalSources.title: WSTC Europe Day 2: Bright smiles, brilliant moves, and cultural rhythms in Tsaghkadzor
additionalSources.summary: The second day of the European Continental Stage of the FIDE ISCF World Schools Team Championship 2026 brought an incredible mix of high energy, team spirit, and pure chess magic to Tsaghkadzor, Armenia. With school teams cheering each other on, Rounds 3 and 4 turned into a wonderful celebration of young talent. While the games on the top tables grew increasingly intense, the friendly handshakes at the end of each round remained as warm as ever. Round 3: Team spirit shines bright As the morning games kicked off, the tournament hall was buzzing with excitement. Our young players have quickly adjusted to the rapid tempo, and Round 3 showed just how well these school teams can work together to solve tricky puzzles on the board. Several matchups delivered high-stakes tactical chaos, critical strategic errors, or overwhelming piece pressure. The game of Svanadze vs. Predin saw a brilliant display of standard attacking patterns against a loosely castled king. Black compromised their center early with the careless blunder (15… d4??), which White capitalized on perfectly. Black’s position was beyond repair, but after 18… Re8??, White executed a thematic piece sacrifice wrapping it up. Svanadze – Predin After 19.Qh5! g6 20.Bxg6! hxg6 21. Qxg6+ Kh8 22.Bg5 Black was forced to give up his queen (1-0). Round 4: Tension builds up The most memorable moment of the day happened in the following game: Simonovic – Khachatryan White built a rock-solid, visually pleasing positional advantage out of the opening (+1.60) but let it slip away, ending up in an equal position. White’s woes did not stop there as he played a disastrous 31. e4?? Black snatched the initiative after 31…fxe4 32. Bxe4 Qe5?! (better was 32…Qd7) and here White blundered again with 33.f3??, handing Black a superior endgame. Black’s conversion was far from perfect, but in the end he scored a full point. Day 2 completely shook up the standings compared to Day 1. It is so exciting to see how much can change in just a couple of games! Gymnasium N 50 of Minsk showed incredible determination. On Day 2, they kept their undefeated streak rolling! Katrina Yakovleva went on a total winning spree, scoring a perfect 2/2 on the day to help her team fly solo at the top of the leader board with 8 total match points! LEPL Georgia (Kutaisi Andria Razmadze Physico) on the rise! The most joyful leap of the day belongs to this team. They had a brilliant Day 2, leapfrogging the Latvian squad to claim the lone 2nd place spot with 7 points. Gabriel Gabadadze was a superstar on board 1, winning both of his Day 2 games to stay completely perfect at 4/4. The “6-point” parking lot! Talk about a crowded finish! Riga State Gymnasium No. 1, Green Village School, C.N. “Costache Negruzzi”, Yerevan’s School N 77, and Tallinna Tonismae Reaalkool all fought like lions on Day 2. They are now locked in a giant tie for 3rd place with 6 points each! Endgame Super-Spurts!: A huge high-five goes to “Mkhitar Sebastatsi” Educational Complex and Osnovna sola Bojana Ilicha Maribor! Both teams had a tough Day 1, but they bounced right back on Day 2, scoring great wins to vault themselves up into the top 10 with 5 match points! Complete standings after Day 2 A day for joy, learning, and new friends Away from the chess clocks, the championship continued to show that every single day is an adventure and a chance to discover something wonderful together. The afternoon shifted the spotlight to fantastic masterclasses and a fun journey into Armenia’s ancient culture, giving the kids the perfect chance to relax, play, and make friends from different countries. The big highlight of the afternoon was a very special masterclass called “Raising Champions: From Talent To Title,” hosted by GM Zaven Andriasian. This unique session was specially designed for the coaches and parents of our future grandmasters. It put a deeply important focus on the psychological training of young players, exploring how to build mental resilience, maintain emotional balance during tense games, and create a supportive environment that helps children navigate both victories and defeats with confidence. Right after the final round of the day the playing hall was filled with laughter during the thrilling “Simul with a Twist” with GM Manuel Petrosyan. The possibility for all the kids to make a decision about next move on the board added a super fun, chaotic energy to the games, challenging the kids to think on their feet and laugh along as they tried to outsmart one of Armenia’s top grandmasters. The afternoon concluded on a beautiful, high-energy artistic note with a lively Armenian Dance Workshop. Swapping chess pieces for lively musical beats, players, coaches, and parents enthusiastically joined hands to learn traditional steps. The activity area quickly transformed into a sea of smiles, happy rhythms, and friendly chaos, completely washing away the competitive tension of the day’s games. What’s Next? As we cross the halfway mark of this wonderful festival, the team standings are incredibly close! The upcoming rounds will bring even more exciting matchups, but no matter what the scoreboard says, the true victory is the fantastic memories and friendships these young chess ambassadors are building here in Tsaghkadzor. Official website: https://worldschoolteam2026.fide.com/

title: Judit Polgar Scores 3.5-1.5 In Simultaneous Display At Global Chess Festival
summary: The 12th edition of GM Judit Polgar's traditional annual Global Chess Festival was staged on September 26 in the Hungarian National Gallery, Budapest. Judit took on five different communities in a simultaneous display, scoring 3.5-1.5, with three wins, a draw, and a loss. Unlike in 2025, when she swept the opposition 6-0, she found the going tougher this year, facing much stiffer resistance. Sponsored by Morgan Stanley, the global financial services company, the festival was themed 'Critical Thinking' for its latest edition and had a number of activities centered on the game. The festival had great local support, as evident from the presence of Zoltan Tanacs, the new Hungarian Minister of Science and Technology. The ceremonial first move of the simul was made by Erno Rubik, inventor of the Rubik's cube. Community simul LIVE - join us! 💃❤Ernő Rubik is with us. 😊Link in comments👇#ChessConnectsUs @MorganStanley #criticalthinking #ChessSimul @chesscom pic.twitter.com/6KkLedkjIm He also presided over a RubikChess Tournament, open to the public, with 10 minutes for each team on the clock. Teams of two competed in a Swiss tournament with one member of the team needing to play chess while the other solved a 3x3 Rubik's cube, working together with an eye on time. Judit started her day with a blindfold game against GM Gergely Antal, a prominent Hungarian player who played for the second team of Hungary just a couple of years ago at the 45th Chess Olympiad in Budapest. The game ended in a draw. One of Judit's older sisters, IM Sofia Polgar, was the guest of honor at the festival this year. She joined Judit and GM Krisztian Szabo on The Master Relay Simul, where a relay of chess masters took turns continuing each other's games. Judit's purely chess event was the Communities Chess Simul against five different teams. Players present at the board were helped by their communities spread all over the world, with move suggestions and analysis through Twitch or a similar platform. Judit had 110 minutes against the teams' 50 minutes, with a 10-second increment added after each move for both sides. The simultaneous display was streamed live, hosted by IM Anna Rudolf. Judit's only loss was against the 'Pietro Chess' Community (belonging to Pietro Checkmate / Pietro Silke Balerna). Also present at the simul was streamer 'Sadistic Tushi' (Tushar Anand) who gave Pietro the interesting suggestion 15...0-0! which was a crucial idea, setting the initial tone of the game. Black sacrifices a second pawn, catching Judit's king in the center.

title: Garry Kasparov Reportedly Warned Of Alleged Russian Assassination Plot In U.S.
summary: The 13th World Chess Champion Garry Kasparov was warned by U.S. authorities this summer that he was the target of a plot to kill him and was placed under special protection, according to Spanish newspaper El Mundo, citing a source close to the former world champion. Spain's second-largest newspaper reported on Wednesday that a network linked to Russian intelligence had been planning attacks on Kasparov and other exiled opponents of Vladimir Putin. It said the alleged plans to kill former Russian lawmaker Ilya Ponomarev in the United States were further advanced. U.S. prosecutors have not publicly named Kasparov as a target in that case, but a source close to the former world champion told El Mundo "US authorities confirmed to him this summer that he is a target." Rusia planificó matar a Kasparov y a otros disidentes este verano en EEUU https://t.co/2mDHBXt1ha pic.twitter.com/pcNaQeJf1H The report comes after the U.S. Justice Department on September 15 revealed that five people had been charged over alleged plots to surveil and kill Russian dissidents and carry out attacks in Europe. Their indictment refers to a dissident in the United States as “Victim-1,” whom El Mundo identifies as Ponomarev. According to prosecutors, a person recruited by the network photographed and filmed locations associated with Victim-1. Two of the defendants then offered that person $40,000 to carry out the killing. The person refused and was asked whether someone else could do it. The five defendants remain at large, and the charges have yet to be proven in court. According to El Mundo, two targets were to be killed in the United States, while another potential victim was targeted in Vilnius, Lithuania. 63-year-old Kasparov was the world chess champion from 1985 to 2000. Although he retired from chess in 2005, he remains involved in the game through his relationship with the Saint Louis Chess Club. There, he recently played a Chess960 match against GM Veselin Topalov, eventually losing 16-8. In recent years, he has become known as one of Putin's most prominent critics. In 2012, he was arrested outside a Moscow court, where he was reportedly subject to police brutality. He left Russia in 2013 and later co-founded the Free Russia Forum, a gathering of Russian opposition figures in Lithuania. Russia designated him a "foreign agent" in 2022, added him to its list of "terrorists and extremists" in 2024, and ordered his arrest in absentia later that year. Russian state-controlled news agency Tass reported in May that Kasparov had been placed on an international wanted list the previous December.
